A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SES research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original supervised, active, and continual learning experiments, together with ablations and qualitative analyses in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark experiments and adds continual learning evaluations, ablations, encoding-tree comparisons, and a synthetic coverage simulation.

M1.justification: The core graph construction, entropy score, multiplication with training difficulty, and blue-noise selector remain unchanged. Limited procedural extensions include batchwise selection with ten-slot merge-reduce replay memory for task-free learning (Appendix F.3) and an evaluated hypergraph-to-graph construction variant (Appendix G).

E1.justification: The existing real-world datasets are retained. v3 substantially extends test scenarios with separately reported task-incremental and task-free continual learning, changing access to task identity and training boundaries (Table 21). Appendix C also adds a Gaussian-mixture simulation with ten classes and 5,000 samples per class.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated k-means and k-DPP baselines to supervised comparisons. Continual learning adds k-center, Gradient Matching, FRCL, DER++, GSS, and GCR (Tables 18–21). Older comparators omitted from the shortened main Table 3 remain in the appendix; the active-learning comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 extends replay-memory budgets from 100/200 to 50/100/200/400 and introduces testing with task identities and training without known task boundaries, including batchwise merge-reduce updates. New analyses use encoding-score correlations and synthetic coverage ratios. Existing dataset splits, optimization settings, and selection-hyperparameter tables are largely retained; these additions do not establish reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices A, C, and G add encoding-tree construction comparisons, synthetic validation of the coverage bound, ablation of the entropy degree term, alternative global/local score combinations, and a hypergraph variant. The original module, difficulty-metric, k-sensitivity, and qualitative analyses are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages over five seeds without accompanying uncertainty values in its benchmark tables. v3 adds extensive ± reporting in Tables 10–21, including retained results. Five-run averaging remains, so an increased run count is not established; the PDFs do not identify whether the new ± quantities are standard deviations, standard errors, or intervals.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive baseline, memory-budget, continual-setting, simulation, and ablation results while retaining most matched headline means. Existing IMDB values also change: SES at 1% changes from 84.04 to 83.14, and Variance at 10% from 49.76 to 92.44 (v1 Table 11; v3 Table 14). New Table 18 reports DER++ at 88.82 versus SES at 81.18 for Permuted MNIST with memory 200, contradicting the retained universal-superiority statement.

T1.justification: v3 adds a formal coverage definition, distributional and bounded-weight assumptions, and a proposed entropy-to-coverage bound with a derivation in Appendix C and Equation 5. It also introduces a coverage-to-loss theorem attributed to Zheng et al. The original Shapley proposition and proof are retained, moving from Appendix A to B.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims about Shapley-based entropy decomposition, combining global and local information, and effectiveness across three learning scenarios. Explicitly mentioning linear-time calculation in the contribution list restates a claim already made in v1.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive arguments connecting entropy, coverage, and model performance, and attributes the hypergraph variant's weaker results to information loss during clique expansion. It also discusses impracticality at billion-sample scale and unresolved dataset partitioning, and distinguishes replay-memory construction from memory-use optimization. Earlier limitations concerning tuning costs and multimodal support remain.

D1.justification: v3 changes the listed implementation access from an anonymous repository to GitHub and adds concrete runtime information: approximately 30 versus 3 minutes for MiniGPT-4 fine-tuning on one V100, plus two seconds of selection overhead. It also documents synthetic-data generation and ten-slot task-free memory handling. Most existing training and hyperparameter details are retained.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens literature coverage around diversity-based sampling, additional continual learning methods, hypergraphs, and large-dataset scalability. Appendix F.3 newly positions SES as memory construction and explains the exclusion of memory-use methods such as GEM. The central global-versus-local motivation remains; bibliographic year corrections alone are not counted.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain. v3 clarifies terminology, expands explanations, adds acknowledgements, subdivides appendix results by learning scenario, and moves two main-text ablations into Appendix G. These are limited editorial and organizational changes alongside the separately assessed scientific additions.

P2.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes result displays: combined appendix benchmark tables are split by dataset and expanded with uncertainty values, the main continual-learning table is condensed, and fuller comparisons and new analyses receive additional tables. The difficulty-metric table and k-sensitivity plot move to the appendix; existing qualitative figures are retained.

improvement.justification: The expanded comparisons and targeted design ablations address gaps in v1's validation and make SES's empirical behavior more assessable. However, the gain is limited by unspecified uncertainty quantities and new reporting inconsistencies: Table 18 contradicts the universal-superiority claim, and Table 24's averages do not match its displayed scores. The added evidence provides a net benefit, but these unresolved issues prevent a clear substantial quality improvement.
